subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: Stem cells are defined by their ability to:
choices: Carry out one specialised function very efficiently for the organism
Divide only once before they become a specialised cell
Fuse with other cells to form tissues with many nuclei
Divide many times and differentiate along different pathways
items.note: The two properties are unlimited division (self-renewal) and the capacity to differentiate.

items.stem: A cell that can differentiate into any cell type of the body, but not into placenta, is described as:
choices: Totipotent
Multipotent
Pluripotent
Unipotent
items.note: Totipotent = every cell type including extra-embryonic (zygote); pluripotent = all body cells (embryonic stem cells); multipotent = a limited range (e.g. blood stem cells).

items.stem: Which is an example of a stem cell niche in an adult human?
choices: Bone marrow
Red blood cells
Skeletal muscle fibres
The lens of the eye
items.note: Two examples to know: bone marrow (blood cells) and hair follicles. A niche is the location that maintains stem cells or promotes their proliferation and differentiation.

items.stem: In an early embryo, cells in different positions develop differently mainly because:
choices: Each cell receives a different set of chromosomes from the zygote
Gradients of signal molecules cause different genes to be expressed
Cells at the edge of the embryo mutate more often than cells in the centre
Cells in the centre receive more oxygen than cells at the edge
items.note: Morphogen gradients switch genes on or off depending on concentration, so position decides the cell's fate. The DNA is the same in each cell.

items.stem: Why do cells divide when they reach a certain size rather than keep growing?
choices: Surface area to volume ratio falls as a cell grows, limiting exchange
Volume to surface area ratio falls as a cell grows, limiting exchange
The nucleus becomes too large to fit inside the cell membrane
The cell wall prevents further growth in all cell types
items.note: As size increases, volume (needs) grows faster than surface area (supply). The SA:V ratio falls, so exchange with the surroundings cannot keep up.

items.stem: A cube-shaped cell has sides of 20 µm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?
items.note: SA = 6 × 20² = 2400 µm²; V = 20³ = 8000 µm³; 2400 ÷ 8000 = 0.3 µm⁻¹. Units cancel to give a ratio of 0.3 : 1.

items.stem: Type I pneumocytes are adapted for gas exchange because they are:
choices: Thick and cuboidal, making surfactant to coat the alveoli
Covered with cilia that sweep mucus out of the lungs
Extremely thin, giving a short diffusion distance
Packed with mitochondria to pump oxygen actively
items.note: Type I cells are flattened, about 0.15 µm thick. Type II cells are cuboidal and secrete surfactant.

items.stem: Which adaptation of a sperm cell is correctly linked to its function?
choices: A large cytoplasm stores yolk to nourish the early embryo
A cortical granule layer prevents polyspermy at fertilisation
A haploid nucleus with two sets of chromosomes for the zygote
Mitochondria in the midpiece supply ATP for the flagellum
items.note: Sperm: small, flagellum, many mitochondria, acrosome with enzymes, haploid nucleus (one set). Yolk and cortical granules belong to the egg.

items.stem: Some cells become very large but keep a high SA:V ratio. Which adaptation achieves this?
choices: Being long and thin, or having a highly folded surface
Being as close to a sphere in shape as possible
Increasing the thickness of the plasma membrane to allow faster exchange
Storing more water in a central vacuole
items.note: A sphere has the lowest SA:V for its volume. Flattening, elongation and folds (microvilli) increase surface area relative to volume.

items.stem: Cardiac muscle cells are connected by intercalated discs. The main function of these is to:
choices: Store the calcium ions that are released each time the heart muscle relaxes
Make the cells multinucleate like skeletal muscle fibres
Prevent ions from passing from one cell to the next
Let electrical impulses pass quickly so the cells contract in sync
items.note: Intercalated discs contain gap junctions (and anchoring junctions), so the impulse spreads cell to cell and the chambers contract together.

items.stem: Which statement about the use of stem cells is correct?
choices: Adult stem cells from bone marrow are totipotent and can form a whole organism
Using cord blood stem cells always requires the destruction of an embryo
Embryonic stem cells have greater potency than adult stem cells but raise more ethical issues
Stem cells from one person can be given to any other person with no risk at all of immune rejection
items.note: Embryonic cells are pluripotent but obtaining them destroys an embryo; adult and cord blood cells are multipotent with fewer ethical issues; mismatched cells can be rejected.

items.stem: Explain the importance of the surface area to volume ratio as a factor limiting cell size.
markscheme: Rate of metabolism / need for exchange depends on volume (1)
Rate of exchange depends on surface area (1)
As the cell grows, volume increases faster than surface area, so SA:V falls (1)
Above a certain size exchange becomes too slow / cell must divide (1)
items.tactic: Ratio questions: say which grows faster and what that means for supply vs demand.

items.stem: Outline how stem cells in the bone marrow maintain the population of red blood cells.
markscheme: Stem cells in the bone marrow niche divide repeatedly (1)
Some daughter cells remain stem cells (self-renewal) (1)
Others differentiate into red blood cells (lose nucleus, make haemoglobin) (1)
This replaces red blood cells that are destroyed after about 120 days (1)
items.tactic: Outline: link the two stem-cell properties to the outcome.

items.stem: Compare the adaptations of red and white blood cells to their functions.
markscheme: Both are made from stem cells in the bone marrow (1)
Red cells lack a nucleus/mitochondria, giving more room for haemoglobin; white cells have a nucleus (1)
Red cells are biconcave for a large SA:V and fast oxygen diffusion (1)
White cells can change shape to squeeze out of capillaries / engulf pathogens (1)
Some white cells make antibodies, needing many ribosomes/rough ER (1)
items.tactic: Compare = similarities and differences, each tied to function.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Cubes of agar containing a pink pH indicator were placed in acid. Acid diffusing in turns the indicator colourless. Cube side (cm) / SA:V (cm⁻¹) / time to fully decolourise (min): 1 / 6.0 / 4; 2 / 3.0 / 15; 3 / 2.0 / 34.
(a) Show that the SA:V ratio of the 3 cm cube is 2.0 cm⁻¹. (b) Describe the relationship between SA:V and the time taken. (c) Use the data to explain why large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces.
markscheme: (b) As SA:V decreases, time increases, and not proportionally: from 6.0 to 2.0 cm⁻¹ time rises from 4 to 34 min (1)
(c) Large organisms have a low SA:V so diffusion to the centre is too slow (1)
Specialised surfaces (e.g. lungs, villi) increase surface area / reduce distance (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
